query.query: can two pytest sessions run at the same time here

items.text:
Two pytest sessions running at the same time against the same test database collide. `tests/conftest.py`
calls `apply_migrations` from a session fixture, and `recall.schema`'s guard refuses the second one:

recall.schema.ConcurrentMigrator: another RE-call schema migrator is already running

The loser does not fail one test. **Every** test errors at setup, so the run reports e.g.
`3 skipped, 62 errors` with no failures at all. Reproduced deliberately on 2026-08-05 with three
concurrent runs of `tests/test_bench_systems.py`: one passed, two errored wholesale.

**How to apply:**
1. A suite verdict is the SUMMARY LINE, never an exit code. An output file with no pytest output
   means "did not run or was lost", whatever the code says.
2. Launch long suites detached with their own log (`nohup python -u -m pytest tests/ -q > log
   2>&1 &`, the `-u` matters or the log stays empty for minutes) and watch the log with a
   Monitor until-loop for the summary line.
3. Before relaunching anything DB-backed, list live python processes and match COMMAND LINES:
   two suites on one session database invalidate each other silently.
4. Distinguish your processes from other sessions' by command line before killing: this machine
   routinely runs parallel sessions with their own suites.

| Symptom | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `ConcurrentMigrator` in fixture setup | two pytest processes contend for the schema-migration advisory lock; `scripts/ablate_store_latency_guards.py` documents it |
| `LockNotAvailable: canceling statement due to lock timeout` | another session on the SAME container, still running |
| `test_rate_limit_http.py`, `test_mcp_auth_http.py` | these stand up real HTTP servers and contend on PORTS; a private container does not protect them |
| `FileNotFoundError` inside `tmp_path` | pytest keeps only the 3 most recent `pytest-of-<user>/pytest-<n>` roots and prunes older ones AT STARTUP, so a new run deletes the dirs of runs in flight |
| pool / latency / backend-count assertions ("pool churned: 3 distinct backends…") | CPU contention, not DB contention |
|

**Why it matters:** the guard is working as designed, but its failure signature looks exactly like a
catastrophic breakage of the code under test. It cost me a wrong conclusion once: in a mutation-testing
harness I counted two mutants as "caught" because the suite went red, when the redness was this
collision and not the mutant.

**How to apply:** run pytest sessions in this repo **sequentially**, never overlapping. In any harness
that shells out to pytest in a loop, treat `errors` and `failed` as different evidence: only `failed`
means a test caught something. Retry (or abort) on seeing `ConcurrentMigrator` in the output rather
than scoring that run. See also [[bench-systems-suite-spends-openrouter-credits]] for the other trap in
this same file.

---

🔑 **The competing process is usually one I started myself.** A `bug-auditor` subagent runs pytest.
Chaining `pytest A && pytest B` overlaps if the first has not fully released its connections. Both
happened repeatedly, and I diagnosed the results as broken apparatus, code regression, catalog
bloat and machine contention before noticing I was the other party. **Tell subagents explicitly not
to touch the database, and never run a suite while one is live.**

🔑 **The failing test set CHANGES every run** and each one passes in isolation, which reads exactly
like order-dependent shared state. There is no randomiser installed — it is whichever test happened
to be migrating when the lock was taken.

**Measured 2026-08-18** on this Windows workstation, with a session container:

```
5694 passed, 32 skipped in 1857.08s (0:30:57)
```

`CLAUDE.md:140` states "The full suite takes about **12 minutes** with a database and about 5
without." That is **stale by a factor of two and a half**, and it is a claim in a file loaded into
every session, so it is believed by default.

## Why it matters beyond the number

A 15 or 20 minute timeout looks generous against the documented figure and **kills the run at
roughly two thirds**. That is exactly what happened here on the first attempt, and the killed run
then reported success because its exit code came from a `| tail` rather than from pytest. Two
independent defects lined up to turn "the suite did not finish" into "the suite passed".

RE-call's DB-backed suite produces failures that have nothing to do with the code under test,
repeatedly and at wildly different scales: 15 failed + 5 errors, 473 errors, 41 failed + 59
errors, 8 failed + 12 errors, and single one-off errors. Every one passed on isolated re-run.
Budget for it: the full suite is 15-20 minutes, so a false red is expensive to chase.

query.query: will re-indexing repair a chunker bug

items.text:
**The chunker is not in it.** So a file whose bytes have not changed is skipped even when the
chunker that would now read it is a different one. Fixing a chunker-selection bug therefore does
**not** repair an affected corpus by re-running `recall index`, the run reports "N unchanged" and
leaves every wrongly-split chunk exactly where it was.

To actually rebuild, change one of the three terms (a different embedder, a different context
policy) or delete the affected sources first and let the next run re-read them.

The source docstring calls widening the tuple out as a migration rather than a comment change,
because it re-fingerprints every indexed corpus at once. That is a real cost and the reason it has
not been done, not an oversight.

query.query: why can I not git checkout master in this repo

items.text:
As of 2026-08-12 this repo has ~18 worktrees. The main checkout at
`C:/Users/gde00/Documents/recall` usually sits on a feature branch (`codex/enterprise-rag-bench`
when this was written), and **`master` is checked out in a separate worktree at
`C:/Users/gde00/Documents/recall-suite-fix`**.

So `git checkout master` from the main checkout fails with *"'master' is already used by worktree
at ..."*. To land work on master, operate on that worktree directly:

```bash
git -C "C:/Users/gde00/Documents/recall-suite-fix" merge --squash <branch>
```

**Why this bit me:** I ran `git checkout master 2>&1 | tail -2 && git merge --squash <branch>`. The
pipe made `&&` read `tail`'s exit status, not the failed checkout's, so the squash merge ran against
the *feature branch* that happened to be checked out, leaving 13 staged additions and two
conflicted files in the user's working tree. `git reset --hard HEAD` restored it because nothing was
committed and the tree had been clean.

**How to apply:** Check `git worktree list` before assuming any branch can be checked out. Never
pipe a command whose exit status gates a `&&` chain; capture the status explicitly instead. And
check the target worktree is clean before merging into it.

**A third form, same root: a squash-merged branch looks unmerged forever.** Squashing rewrites the
content into one new commit, so the source branch's original commits are never ancestors of master
and `git log origin/master..HEAD` keeps listing them. "5 commits ahead of master" on such a branch
is not evidence of pending work.

Measured 2026-08-18: I merged master into `claude/enterprise-rag-dense-floor`, reported it as "worth
a second merge before it goes in", and only checked afterwards that its PR #334 had been **merged

across 14 files, not the 4 commits the log showed. Ask the forge, not the commit graph:

matters, at the START and again before merging, and read it as a supersession signal:

items.text:
- Prefer the Edit tool for file changes; it does not do this.
- If scripting an edit in Python, pass `newline="\n"`:
  `path.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8", newline="\n")`.
- To diagnose: `git ls-files --eol <file>` shows index vs working-tree endings directly.
- To confirm a diff is line-endings-only, hash both sides normalised rather than trusting
  `git diff --ignore-all-space`, which also hides real whitespace changes:
  `git show HEAD:f | tr -d '\r' | sha256sum` against `tr -d '\r' < f | sha256sum`.
- To fix once content is confirmed identical: `git checkout -- <files>`. Do NOT commit it; the
  commit would record no content change.

Related: [[ruff-blocked-locally]] for the other local tooling gotcha in this repo.

⚠️ Same session, a second way a "successful" write leaves the wrong state, unrelated to concurrency.

query.query: is it enough for a guard to refuse known-bad values

items.text:
**Refusing known-BAD values is a negative check. It closes only the failure modes you thought of,
and everything the producer never emits — or that predates the field — walks straight through.**

Measured, RE-call `fix/beam-artifact-rejudgeable`, 2026-08-07. I wrote `embed_parity.py` to stop a
GPU-vs-CPU comparison silently running CPU-vs-CPU. Three guards in it could not fire:

🔑 The closed form is `if meta.get("providers_source") != "session": refuse` — require the
known-good value. It rejects nothing the producer emits and everything it does not.

🔑 **A test that hand-crafts an input the producer cannot produce is not a test of the guard.**
That is how #3 shipped green.

↔ Same family as [[feedback-a-guard-that-reads-as-protection-and-cannot-fire-2026-07-30]] and
[[feedback-check-the-deciding-cell-has-power-2026-08-06]]. What is new here is the *repair*
inheriting the defect, and that only an audit by other agents caught it.

- **A pre-filter may be sloppy; a decision may not.** The `case` in `settings.json` that decides
  whether to *invoke* a guard can over-match harmlessly, because the script then decides. The script
  itself cannot.
- **One residual false positive is known and left in place.** Backticks inside single quotes are not
  command substitution to a shell, but the parser treats them as such. It over-detects, which is the
  safe direction for a guard, and it is documented rather than silently accepted.

Related: [[test-a-guards-allow-path]] is the same session's other half, a guard refusing correct
work. [[guards-that-cannot-fail]] is the opposite failure. [[a-detector-with-no-sink]] completes the
set: fires and is discarded, fires wrongly, never fires.

- **Enumerate mutants from the SOURCE, top to bottom, not from the guards you remember.** I once
  mutated 25 guards, reached 24/25 and called it verified; an auditor enumerated from the file,
  ran 51, and 26 survived, including the identity cross-check the whole design existed for
  (it compared one of its four columns) and a type loop whose deletion makes a bad row *served as
  a hit* rather than refused.
- **A guard with a long comment defending it is a positive signal it is untested.** The author
  explained it instead of pinning it. `rollback()`, a `close()` on the refusal path, and an mkdir
  block were each argued for at length and pinned by nothing.
- **A guard with N conjoined terms needs N tests, one per term.** A single test can only ever see
  one term, because it varies one

⚠️ Note the asymmetry that makes this dangerous: a cannot-fail guard produces a **false green**,
and a cannot-pass guard produces a **false red** that discards good work. I produced one of each in
the same session.

query.query: what should I check before replacing NOPASSWD sudo with an allowlist

items.text: Before deploying any sudoers lockdown that replaces wildcard `NOPASSWD: ALL` with a Cmnd_Alias allowlist, **verify whether the target user has a password set**. Without one, sudo for any non-allowlisted command silently fails with "a terminal is required to read the password" — the operator is locked out of every ad-hoc admin operation, and even console root login becomes the only recovery path.

**How to apply:**
- Step 0 (always): `sudo passwd -S <user>` (or `sudo grep <user>: /etc/shadow | cut -d: -f2`) — if it shows `L` / `*` / empty hash, no password is set.
- If no password: ask the operator before deploy, *"do you want me to set a password first (so non-allowlist commands prompt + work) or accept that the allowlist is a hard wall?"*. Do not assume.
- Even when a password exists, double-check the operator can recover via console — every Cmnd_Alias deploy needs a documented break-glass path that's been tested.
- Keep the pre-deploy file backup at a path the new sudoers still permits to read (so post-deploy rollback to the prior policy is possible from the same shell). The 2026-05-05 deploy left the backup at `/etc/sudoers.d/90-sentiment.bak.<TS>` — DENIED to read by the new

**Why:** 2026-05-05 redteam fix session. Saw `/etc/sudoers.d/90-sentiment: sentiment ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL` and assumed "NOPASSWD" implied "no password set". Deployed Cmnd_Alias lockdown. User immediately hit `[sudo] password for sentiment:` prompts when running outside the allowlist (e.g., `tee /etc/contabo/credentials.env`, `docker compose up -d` for a config refresh). The password actually *was* set, but the user couldn't remember it — equivalent to no fallback. Recovery options collapsed to (a) Contabo VNC console root login (operator did not have access at that moment) or (b) a destructive snapshot revert (the 2026-05-05 attempt got 400/404 from the Contabo API depending on body shape — `{}` body returns 404 'Cannot POST', empty body returns 400 'body cannot be empty').
